title: Class 6 Maths Probability: Chance, Events & Simple Probability + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Probability Explained + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Class 6 maths probability made simple: certain, impossible and likely events, plus favourable-over-total sums for coins, dice and bags, with a free quiz.
excerpt: Will it rain tomorrow? Will a tossed coin land heads? Class 6 probability is where children first put a number on chance. Here is how the chapter works, with two solved case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Class 6 student whether the sun will rise tomorrow and they will say yes without blinking. Ask whether a rolled die will show a 4 and the answer gets slower — ‘maybe?’ That gap between ‘definitely’ and ‘maybe’ is exactly where class 6 maths probability begins. The chapter takes the everyday word chance and teaches children to sort events, compare them, and finally put a number on how likely something is.

I have taught this chapter to eleven-year-olds in a few Tier-2 city classrooms, and the single biggest win is realising that probability is not about predicting the future. It is about describing how likely an outcome is, before it happens. Once that clicks, the rest of the chapter falls into place.

The idea of chance

Everything around us is either sure to happen, sure not to happen, or somewhere in between. A ball dropped from your hand will fall. Your maths teacher turning into a parrot will not. Rain on a July afternoon in Pune? That sits in the messy middle. Class 6 asks children to notice this spread and give each situation a fair label.

Certain, impossible, likely, unlikely, equally likely

The chapter sorts events into a few honest categories. Getting these words right matters more than any calculation at this stage.

  • Certain — it must happen. The day after Monday is Tuesday.
  • Impossible — it cannot happen. Rolling a 7 on an ordinary six-faced die.
  • Likely — a good chance, but not guaranteed. Drawing a red marble from a bag that holds 9 red and 1 blue.
  • Unlikely — a small chance. Drawing that single blue marble.
  • Equally likely — two outcomes with the same chance. Heads or tails on a fair coin.

A quick caveat I share with students: ‘unlikely’ does not mean ‘never’. That blue marble can still come out on the first try. Rare is not the same as impossible, and children mix these up constantly.

Class 6 maths probability: putting a number on it

Here is the one formula the chapter builds towards. The probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes, when every outcome is equally likely.

Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.

Toss a coin: there are 2 equally likely outcomes and 1 is heads, so the chance of heads is 1 out of 2. Roll a die: 6 outcomes, and getting a 4 is 1 of them, so 1 out of 6. The counter-intuitive bit for many students is that a probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain) — you can never be ‘150% sure’, however confident you feel.

Case study 1: the spinner and the die

Riya spins a spinner split into 4 equal coloured parts – red, blue, green and yellow – and also rolls a fair die. Read the passage, then work the questions.

  • What is the chance the spinner lands on green? There are 4 equal parts and green is 1 of them, so 1 out of 4.
  • Is landing on red or blue more likely than landing on green? No. Each colour is 1 of 4, so all four are equally likely.
  • What is the probability the die shows a number greater than 4? The favourable outcomes are 5 and 6, that is 2 of the 6 faces, so 2 out of 6.
  • Is rolling an odd number on the die certain, impossible, or equally likely to an even number? Odd numbers are 1, 3, 5 and even are 2, 4, 6 — three each, so the two are equally likely.

Case study 2: the bag of marbles

A cloth bag holds 5 red marbles, 3 green marbles and 2 yellow marbles, all the same size. Aarav draws one marble without looking. Total marbles = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.

  • Probability of drawing a red marble? 5 favourable out of 10, so 5 out of 10 — that is a half.
  • Which colour is least likely? Yellow, with only 2 out of 10.
  • Is drawing a black marble possible? No. There are no black marbles, so this is impossible — probability 0.
  • Is drawing a red, green or yellow marble certain? Yes. Every marble is one of those three colours, so it is certain — probability 1.

Notice how both case studies lean on the same two skills: count the favourable outcomes, count the total, and then read the label off the number. That pattern is the whole chapter in one sentence, and it is why solved case studies are such useful practice — each passage forces a child to choose what to count.

quiz.title: Class 6 Probability Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on chance, event types and simple probability with coins, dice and bags. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 probability — chance and simple probability

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed. What is the probability of getting heads?
questions.explanation: A coin has 2 equally likely outcomes, heads and tails, and 1 is heads, so the probability is 1 out of 2.

questions.q: Which of these events is impossible?
options: Rolling a 7 on an ordinary die
Drawing a red marble from a bag of red marbles
questions.explanation: An ordinary die has faces 1 to 6 only, so a 7 can never come up. Its probability is 0.

questions.q: A die is rolled. What is the probability of getting an even number?
questions.explanation: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6 — that is 3 favourable outcomes out of 6, so 3 out of 6.

questions.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Which colour is more likely to be drawn?
questions.explanation: There are more blue marbles (6) than red (4), so drawing blue is more likely.

questions.q: Which event is certain to happen?
options: The day after Sunday is Monday
questions.explanation: The day after Sunday is always Monday, so it is certain — probability 1.

questions.q: A spinner has 4 equal parts: red, blue, green and yellow. What is the probability it lands on blue?
questions.explanation: There are 4 equal parts and blue is 1 of them, so the probability is 1 out of 4.

questions.q: A bag holds 5 red, 3 green and 2 yellow marbles. What is the probability of drawing a yellow marble?
questions.explanation: There are 2 yellow marbles out of 10 total (5 + 3 + 2), so the probability is 2 out of 10.

questions.q: Choosing heads or tails on a fair coin is an example of outcomes that are:
questions.explanation: Heads and tails have the same chance on a fair coin, so they are equally likely outcomes.

faq.q: What does probability mean in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: It is a way of describing how likely an event is before it happens. In Class 6 children learn to sort events as certain, impossible, likely, unlikely or equally likely, and to write simple probability as favourable outcomes out of total outcomes.

faq.q: What is the formula for simple probability?
faq.a: Probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes, when every outcome is equally likely. For heads on a coin that is 1 out of 2; for a 4 on a die it is 1 out of 6.

faq.q: What is the difference between an impossible and an unlikely event?
faq.a: An impossible event can never happen and has probability 0, such as rolling a 7 on a normal die. An unlikely event has a small chance but can still happen, like drawing the single blue marble from a bag of ten.

faq.q: Why do coins, dice and marbles appear so often in this chapter?
faq.a: They are simple objects with a fixed, countable list of equally likely outcomes, which makes them perfect for practising the favourable-over-total idea. Once a child can count outcomes for a die, real-world questions become much easier.
